---
title: Design Decisions
---

Several choices in the format and the hooks could reasonably have gone another way. This page
records each one, the alternatives that were considered, and the reason the current choice won.
Where a measurement decided the question, the number is here; where a principle decided it, the
principle is.


## Clearsigned, Not Encoded

The first draft of the format put the instruction inside a base64 payload with a human-readable
preview above it. That is the shape the original project plan suggested. It has a flaw that is
obvious once seen: the preview can be edited while the signed text stays hidden, so a reader can be
shown one thing while the verifier checks another.

The current format is a clearsign, in the manner of an OpenPGP clearsigned message. The
instruction stays in plain text between `BEGIN SIB SIGNED INSTRUCTION` and `BEGIN SIB SIGNATURE`,
and a detached signature follows. There is one copy of the instruction, it is what people read,
and it is what the signature covers. Nothing in the block is opaque except the signature itself.

The cost is that the text is exposed to whatever Slack, email and editors do to it. That cost is
paid by the [canonicalization](../components/canonicalization.qmd) rule, which is deliberately
aggressive about whitespace and typographic substitutions, and by the transport tests that apply
those transformations and assert the block still verifies.


## A Detached JWS, Not a Bespoke Signature

The signature is a JWS compact serialization with an unencoded, detached payload
([RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515) with
[RFC 7797](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7797), `b64: false`), so it reads
`header..signature` with an empty middle segment. The signing input is the base64url header, a
dot, and the canonical instruction text.

A format of the project's own would have been shorter to describe. The JWS was chosen because a
third party can verify the dev-mode path with any JWS library that supports EdDSA and RFC 7797,
because the standards mapping the project plan asks for is then direct, and because an off-the-shelf
construction has had more eyes on it than a new one ever will. The WebAuthn path needs custom
verification either way, since an assertion signs authenticator data rather than the payload, but
that is confined to one algorithm value.


## Short Header Names

The header uses the JOSE and JWT registered names: `alg`, `typ`, `kid`, `b64`, `crit`, `iss`, `iat`,
`exp`, `jti`, `aud`. Two fields are the project's own, `canon` and `mode`, and they are short to
match. Full words were considered, and the documentation is for an international audience where
abbreviations cost something.

Four of the names are not negotiable if the JWS is to remain a JWS: a standard library keys on
`alg`, `kid`, `b64` and `crit`, and rejects a header that renames them. The remaining names are JWT
claim names that no JWS library interprets, so renaming them would have cost nothing in
interoperability. Consistency won: a header that mixes `alg` with `expires_at` is harder to read
than one that speaks a single dialect, and the standard already uses these names. The
[specification](../../spec/format.qmd) expands every field in a table beside the header, so a reader
meets each abbreviation with its meaning.

Longer names would not have lengthened the signature, which is fixed at 64 bytes for both
algorithms. They would have added about one 64-column line to the encoded header.


## Canonicalization Named in the Signed Header

The canonicalization rule that maps the instruction to the bytes that were signed is named in the
header as `canon`, and the header is covered by the signature. The verifier applies exactly that
rule and never guesses.

The alternative, a single fixed rule or a rule chosen by the verifier, fails in two ways. A rule
that collapses whitespace is wrong for JSON, where it changes string values while ignoring key order
and number formatting that do not matter; JSON needs [RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785).
And a rule chosen outside the signature is an attack surface: an attacker could relabel a block to
whichever rule makes a modified text collapse onto the signed form. Naming the rule in the
protected header ties the mapping to the signature, in the way JWS ties `alg` to it.

The list is closed and versioned: `text/1`, `raw/1` and the reserved `json/1`. A rule never
changes in place; a change is a new version, so old signatures keep verifying under the rule they
named. Each rule is its own collision analysis, which is the argument for keeping the list short.
`canon` is deliberately not listed in `crit`: a generic JWS library would reject a header with an
unknown critical parameter, and canonicalization happens in the SIB layer before the bytes reach the
library.


## SIB Takes No Permission Decision

The first implementation gated: a pattern named the actions that needed a verified instruction, and
a PreToolUse hook refused a call when none covered it, consulting a classifier of its own when one
did. That has been removed, and the three decisions below are superseded by its removal. They are
kept because the reasoning that produced them is still the reasoning that argues against bringing
it back.

A gate rebuilds judgement the harness already performs. Claude Code has a permission system with
rules and a classifier; a second pattern-matcher and a second classifier beside it is a parallel
implementation of the same thing, with its own gaps and its own policy file to keep outside the
repository. The specification never described any of it. What SIB uniquely provides is the one
thing a classifier cannot do for itself, which is to verify a signature and say who wrote what.

The cost is recorded in [Threat Model](threat-model.qmd) and measured in
[What the Classifier Sees](what-the-classifier-sees.qmd): refusing forged authority survives the
removal, conveying genuine authority does not.


### Superseded: the hook never returns `allow`

Claude Code's documentation says a PreToolUse hook `allow` is still checked by the auto-mode
classifier. Phase 0's allow-bypass test saw the opposite in the one case it produced: the classifier
denied 5 of 5 baseline deploy attempts, but with the hook returning `allow` the single attempt was
not denied and it deployed. One attempt is thin evidence. The consequence of being wrong in one
direction is a bypass of the harness's own safety layer; in the other direction it is an extra
classifier call. So when a verified instruction covered an action, the hook returned no decision.
With no hook returning a decision at all, the question no longer arises.


### Superseded: a deterministic deny with no verified spans

The original plan called the classifier on every gated tool call. The hook instead denied
deterministically when the manifest held no verified span, without a model call. The policy fixed
the answer in that case: authority flows only from verified spans, and there were none. Calling a
model to confirm a conclusion the policy already dictates would have added latency and a failure
mode for no information.


### Superseded: harness-provided recent activity

Signed instructions carry conditions. Alice's instruction in the tutorial says "once the test suite
passes", and the shipped classifier saw only the policy, the manifest and the tool call. In Phase 1
it answered `ask` on the first gated call in 10 of 10 runs because it had no way to check the
condition, and in a headless run an `ask` is a denial.

The hook then supplied the harness's own record of the last few tool calls with their result status
and a short output tail: observations the harness made, not text the agent chose. With that record
in view, the classifier allowed the covered deploy on the first call in 10 of 10 runs. The
principle survives the removal even though the plumbing does not, and it is now a rule in the
[reference policy](../../spec/classifier-policy.qmd): a condition stated in a verified span is
checked against what the harness recorded, never against the agent's account of what it did.


## The Audience Comes From the Environment

The identifier a harness presents to the verifier is configuration, not content of the repository.
It arrives in `SIB_AUDIENCE`. An earlier version read it from a file in the checkout along with the
gated-action list, and during Phase 1 the model read that file while exploring and changed its own
behavior, which masked the gate in the measurements. An attacker who can edit the repository could
have edited it as easily. Anything that decides what a signature is worth belongs where the agent
cannot reach it.


## The Prompt Tells the Model What Is Verified

The plan reserved `additionalContext` for the model and nothing else, and that is still its role.
Phase 1 added a use for it at prompt time: the UserPromptSubmit hook lists the verified instructions
in context, in model-facing text. Without it, Sonnet 5 saw a signed block it did not understand and
asked for confirmation instead of acting on an instruction that covered the task. The note is
information for the model; the classifier's channel remains the PostToolUse note, and the
[measurements](what-the-classifier-sees.qmd) show the two are not interchangeable.


## Dev Mode Is Explicit

Software keys exist because the hooks, the verifier and the scenarios have to be built and tested
before biometric signing does. They are labelled everywhere. A dev-mode key signs with `mode: "dev"`
in the header, every signing and verification prints a warning that the signature proves possession
of a file rather than the presence of a person, and in enforced mode a dev block reports
`dev_key_in_enforced_mode` and confers nothing. The alternative, an unlabelled testing path that
happens to work in production, is how a prototype's shortcuts become a deployment's holes.
